intro: A fifth-grade store sells every pencil it has by ten o'clock. A truck of corn leaves a farm near Peoria and ends up on a ship bound for Japan. Both stories are about the same two questions. Why can't everyone have everything they want? And why do people in different places make, grow and buy such different things?

The first chapter is about money and choices. You will meet producers and consumers, learn why a price goes up when something runs out, and see what banks, taxes and budgets are for. You will find out why Illinois grows corn while Florida grows oranges, and why trading makes both places better off.

The second chapter is about the land itself. You will learn to read a map with latitude, longitude and scale. Then you will travel through the five regions of the United States, from the rocky Northeast to the deserts of the Southwest, and look closely at the Midwest and Illinois. By the end, you will be able to explain how the land under a place shapes the jobs, food and dangers of the people who live there.
bigQuestion: How do scarce resources and the shape of the land decide what people make, trade and do where they live?

timeline.t: Adam Smith publishes The Wealth of Nations, explaining how markets and self-interest feed a city
Congress orders the land north of the Ohio River measured into square townships, the grid you see from a plane over Illinois
The Louisiana Purchase makes the whole Mississippi River an American highway to the sea
Illinois becomes a state, with a straight northern border drawn to include the shore of Lake Michigan
The Illinois and Michigan Canal opens, linking Lake Michigan to the Illinois River by water
The first railroad across the whole country is finished, tying the West to the Midwest and East
Katharine Lee Bates publishes America the Beautiful after a train trip across the regions
After thousands of banks close, the government begins insuring savers' bank accounts
Congress funds the Interstate Highway System, the roads that now carry trucks between regions
The Mississippi River floods for months, covering farms and towns along the Illinois shore
The census counts about 12.8 million people in Illinois, most of them in the Chicago area

words.d: a person or business that makes goods or does services that others want
a person who buys or uses goods and services
not having enough of something to do everything people want
the next best thing you give up when you make a choice
how much of something sellers are ready to sell at a price
how much of something people want and are able to buy at a price
something everyone can use and share, like a road or a park, that taxes pay for
focusing on making the thing you can do best
lines that measure how far north or south a place is from the equator
an area where the places share features like land, weather or history
something useful found in nature, like soil, water, trees, fish or oil
a center where many routes come together

test.q: A truck driver carries bread to a store. What is the driver?
test.why: The driver does work others want, so the driver is a producer of a service.

test.q: Which of these is a service?
test.why: A service is work done for someone else. A bus ride is work the driver does for you.

test.q: Jalen picks basketball over piano for his free hour. What is the piano practice?
test.why: The opportunity cost is the next best thing given up when you choose.

test.q: When the price of a good goes down, what usually happens to demand?
test.why: Lower prices lead people to buy more. That is the pattern the lesson calls a law.

test.q: The school store had few pencils and many buyers. What did that cause?
test.why: A shortage happens when buyers want more than sellers have at that price.

test.q: Why does a savings account grow a little each year?
choices: The bank pays interest to savers
test.why: Banks lend savers' money and share some of the interest with the savers.

test.q: Which of these is paid for by taxes and shared by everyone?
test.why: Fire protection is a public good. Taxes pay for it and everyone is protected.

test.q: Why does Florida, not Illinois, grow oranges?
test.why: Orange trees die in a hard freeze, and Florida winters stay warm.

test.q: Sam trades extra grapes for Leo's extra crackers. What is true?
test.why: Trade lets each person give up an extra and get something wanted, so both gain.

test.q: Chicago is at about forty-two degrees north. What kind of line is that?
test.why: Latitude measures degrees north or south of the equator.

test.q: Which map shows mountains and rivers but no state lines?
test.why: A physical map shows what nature made, not the borders people drew.

test.q: Which region is flat, has rich soil and grows corn and soybeans?
test.why: Glaciers left the Midwest flat with dark soil, making it the nation's grain heartland.

test.q: Which region has the Grand Canyon, deserts and the Rio Grande?
test.why: The Southwest is mostly dry, with the Colorado River's Grand Canyon and the Rio Grande border.

test.q: Why does Illinois corn travel by barge instead of truck the whole way?
choices: Barges move heavy loads for the least cost
test.why: One barge carries as much as about sixty trucks, so it is the cheapest way to move grain.

test.q: Why do Illinois schools practice tornado drills?
choices: Drills are required in every country
Tornadoes are the hazard most likely in Illinois
test.why: People prepare for the hazard most likely in their region, and the Midwest gets tornadoes.

write.prompt: Make a claim: Is Illinois a better place for a farm or for a big city? Use evidence from both chapters, such as the soil, the rivers, the climate, Chicago's railroads and what prices and trade do, to support your claim.
tips: Start with one clear sentence that says your claim: farm, city or both.
Use at least two facts from the reading as evidence, like the glacier soil, the Illinois Waterway or the railroads that meet in Chicago.
Explain your reasoning: tell why each fact supports your claim, not just what the fact is.
Give the other side one fair sentence. What would someone who disagrees say?
End by saying what the land and the market together make possible in Illinois.
